scope: 3.1.1. Identification of the most influential variables on ammonia removal

missing_ignored: 99 values from Table 3 (descriptive statistics of 14 variables: Min, Max, Median, Mean, SD, Variance, Coef Var, Coef Skewness) belonging to Section 2.2, spliced into Section 3.1.1 text due to PDF page 5 layout

matched: ANN and PCA models developed and applied to identify key factors affecting ammonia removal in MBR
ANN architecture presented with 13 input variables, 2 hidden layers (12 and 7 neurons), 1 output layer, synaptic weights and bias terms (Fig. 3)
ANN performance: low MAE (order 10^-2) and MSE (order 10^-4), rapid convergence in initial epochs indicating strong adaptation and pattern learning (Fig. 4)
PCA scree plot: first three principal components satisfy both Kaiser criterion (eigenvalues > 1) and scree test elbow point (Fig. 5a)
First 3 PCs explain 55% of total variation with R^2 = 0.772; adding more PCs beyond 3 does not justify increased complexity (Fig. 5b)
Sensitivity analysis with ANN identifies ranking of relative importance among top 10 variables for ammonia removal (Fig. 6)
PCA loading plot displays correlations between variables and ammonia removal via angular relationships (0 deg positive, 90 deg uncorrelated, 180 deg negative) (Fig. 7)
Both models identify SRT, operating temperature, and influent ammonia concentration as having the greatest positive impact on ammonia removal
Both models identify influent COD, influent oil and grease (OG), and membrane permeability as having the strongest negative impact on ammonia removal
Comparison with Zhang, Chen, Jiang: agreement on COD as main influential factor, disagreement on influent ammonia influence
Ammonia concentration influence mechanism: accelerates nitrification kinetics and nitrifier growth via Monod kinetics, increasing oxidized ammonia load
Temperature influence mechanism: nitrifier growth rate increases exponentially with temperature; aligns with Leite refinery wastewater findings
pH negative correlation mechanism: nitrification produces H+ ions as final product, decreasing pH as a function of alkalinity

SRT positive correlation mechanism: MBR uncouples SRT from HRT allowing higher SRT, better sludge acclimatization, complete biomass retention, and sufficient growth time for slow-growing nitrifiers before washout
Influent COD negative correlation mechanism: high C/N ratio stimulates heterotrophic bacteria growth, competing for DO and substrate, inhibiting nitrifiers

Experimental evidence from Sepehri & Sarrafzadeh (NAS 100% vs CAS 43% ammonia removal, 37.5 vs 6.6 mg/L nitrate) and Brasil et al. (lower C/N favors nitrifiers); tested MBR operates at high C/N (20.0 ± 11.1)
Influent OG toxic inhibition mechanism: nitrifiers inhibited even at low toxic compound levels; Qin et al. (20-40% removal at 53-153 mg/L OG, >20 mg/L threshold); tested MBR OG up to 48 mg/L
Membrane permeability negative impact mechanism: higher permeability shortens HRT, leaving insufficient contact time for nitrifiers; Song et al. (HRT < 6.5 days reduces N removal)
HRT microbial community impact: Ni et al. showed HRT critical for microbial community structure (0.40 and 0.05 μm pore sizes at 25 °C)
Sludge filterability vs MLVSS: MLVSS has low relative importance, confirming biomass quantity alone is insufficient; filterability relates to nitrifier abundance (NAS twice as filterable as CAS)
